explanation: Fires on an opening quotation mark (", ', “, «, or =" / ']=") that begins a quoted string, either a string literal in code (SQL, JS, Python) or quoted speech or terms in prose (e.g. said: 'I ..., so-called "...). Strongest in code string literals; tokens that are not an opening quote barely fire.

Mixed. It fires on 'terms' in GPL/LGPL license boilerplate ('under the terms of'), on subword or identifier continuations in code (Subclass, Controller, Framework, :, .com), on date separators, and on assorted prose tokens such as 'there' and 'them'. No single shared feature is visible.

Fires diffusely on mid-sentence tokens in descriptive prose, often medical or clinical text (acute, the, by, mitral, sinus) and sometimes narrative text (slowly, delicious, frustration). There is no clear token or context rule, so strength is hard to predict.

Fires on an abstract or general head noun right after 'the' or a quantifier that is about to be qualified by a following 'of' phrase or relative clause (the period of, the time of, the findings of, any information appearing, the name I have set, the direction of). It is weaker on concrete nouns or when no modifier follows.

Fires on scattered tokens in prose, often SEO-spam or awkwardly written text (be able, you can, means, total, former, understanding) and some code imports. There is no consistent token or context pattern.

A mixture. It fires on attribute or module accesses in code (tf.nn, self.box), MATLAB/VBA syntax tokens ([, (, end), spreadsheet cell references, and assorted prose words (Congress, State, Slot, to, script). None of these share an obvious feature.

Fires most strongly on kanji inside Japanese personal names (the given-name characters after a surname, e.g. 小松[政]夫, 中島[哲]也). It also fires on unrelated tokens: subword pieces of technical words (helically, corrugator, microliters), hyphens and digits in dates or measurements, and the pronoun 'I' in self-descriptive text.

Fires on the second piece of a compound or multi-token term, often a journal-name part (Journal of Neuroscience Methods, Neuropsychologia, Med. Chem, Cell Host Microbe) or a positional or relational word (on top, lower half, behind, upon, superimposing, sequentially). Many weaker hits are unrelated.

Fires on a word-initial subword token 'le', 'al' or 'med' (any case, including after a hyphen, slash or dot) that starts a longer word split into pieces: psycho-le-ptic, -le-ader, le-athery, al-derman, al-veolus, Med-iation, med-ulla, /el-asticsearch. The same letters as a whole word, or other subword starts, give little activation.

Fires on the predictable next token of fixed formulaic phrases: generated math questions ('prime factors [of]', 'round to the [nearest]', 'common denominator [of]'), license strings (GPL-3.[0], ShareA[like]), 'squamous [cell]', Go 'import (' and stack-trace 'at'. These are several template types with no shared meaning.

Fires mainly on byte-fragment tokens of multi-byte characters (partial CJK, mojibake, emoji bytes) and on CJK text. It also fires on runs of zeros and on some code punctuation or identifiers (System.Text, badge, ?, ;). Ordinary English words give near zero.

Fires on mid-word subword pieces of rare proper names, foreign words, or Latin and technical terms (jal-ur, trans-es-ophageal, orbicular-is, G-arc-ia, Pop-ulus, Brjáns-d-óttir), often the second or third fragment of a word the tokenizer splits. Common English words do not fire.

Fires on commas and connective tokens in scientific or argumentative prose at the boundary after an evidential or contrastive lead-in or a stated finding (In fact[,], Indeed[,], However[,], 'has been shown [in]', 'a number [of] studies'), where a further claim about evidence is about to follow. It is weak in non-expository text.

A mixture. It fires on CJK and Devanagari byte fragments, Javadoc/JSDoc tags (@version, @fileoverview), tilde approximations (\~20%), box-drawing characters, email or path fragments, and assorted code identifiers. No shared concept is visible.
